## Previously ...

In Lecture 2 you connected `insta-data.csv` to Tableau Public, explored dimensions and measures, and built your first worksheets.

Two of them reported an average, and you found:

- **Mean reach**: 9,788
- **Median reach**: 5,184

. . .

Why is there a near 2-to-1 gap between them?

**Today: When is an average a lie, how do we describe marketing data honestly, and how do we design high-scoring Tableau dashboards?**

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Explain why you must **plot a distribution before summarising it**.
- Select the honest summary for **skewed, zero-inflated marketing metrics** (Mean vs Median vs Mode, IQR vs SD, p50/p90).
- Master the **Four Families of Figures** (Composition, Distribution, Comparison, Relationship) conceptually and in Tableau.
- Implement the **Five Principles of Data Visualization** (Claus Wilke) for ethical, clear design.
- Identify and critique **misleading graphs** in media and corporate reporting.
- Assemble interactive, high-scoring **Tableau Dashboards** meeting the four assignment criteria.

# 1. When an Average Is a Lie

## The 2-to-1 Gap

In your `insta-data.csv` worksheet:

- Mean reach = **9,788**
- Median reach = **5,184**

. . .

If a client asks: *"What is the typical reach of our posts?"* which number do you report?

. . .

If you answer **9,788**, you describe a post that almost never happens. 

If you answer **5,184**, you ignore the breakout viral reels that drove the brand's growth this quarter.

> Choosing a summary statistic is not a calculation; it is a **business claim**.

## Same Summary, Different Data {.smaller}

Four datasets. Identical means ($\bar{x} = 9.0, \bar{y} = 7.5$), identical variances, identical correlation ($r = 0.816$), and identical regression line ($y = 3.00 + 0.500x$).

. . .

Plotted, they are a line, a curve, an outlier, and a vertical cluster!

![Source: [MGT 100 Customer Analytics, UC San Diego](https://github.com/kennethcwilbur/mgt100) (CC BY 4.0)](./figures/external/mgt100_same_stats_different_graphs.png){fig-align="center" height="255px"}

. . .

This is Anscombe's quartet (1973), and its modern descendant, the **Datasaurus Dozen** (Matejka & Fitzmaurice, 2017), which produces a dinosaur with the same summary stats as a cloud of noise.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If summary statistics cannot distinguish a dinosaur from a circle, what are you claiming when you report an average and stop?
:::

## The Golden Rule

**Plot the distribution before you compute a summary of it.**

. . .

Not as a courtesy to the client. As a reality-check on yourself.

. . .

When the histogram appears, answer four questions:

1. **Where is the mass?** One lump, two, or a long tail?
2. **Where is the floor?** How much data sits at or near zero?
3. **What is the ceiling?** Is something capping the values artificially?
4. **What is on the far right?** A VIP customer, or a corrupted row?

## Marketing Data: Skewed & Zero-Inflated {.smaller}

| Metric | Typical Shape | Why the Spike at Zero? |
|---|---|---|
| **Session duration** | Heavily right-skewed | Bounced visits recorded as 0 seconds |
| **Order value** | Heavily right-skewed | >97% of sessions purchase nothing (€0) |
| **Pages per session** | Right-skewed | Single page bounce and gone |
| **Time to conversion** | Long tail | Most visitors never convert |
| **Revenue per user** | Extreme power-law | Handful of "whales" drive the business |

. . .

:::: {layout="[1.2,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

**The bell curve is the rare exception in marketing, never the default.**

Research on digital platforms reveals **3% to 5% of users generate 50%+ of net revenue**. A mean computed across this distribution describes nobody.

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/external/mgt100_revenue_by_customer_rank.png){style="max-height:220px;"}

:::
::::

## Which Summary, When? {.smaller}

:::: {layout="[1,1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

**Mean**

Sum divided by count.

Pulled by extreme values and corrupted rows.

**Right for**: Totals, budgets, financial projections ($n \times \text{mean} = \text{total}$).

:::

::: {#second-column}

**Median**

The 50th percentile (middle value).

Completely unaffected by the size of extreme tails.

**Right for**: "What does a typical user or session experience?"

:::

::: {#third-column}

**Mode**

The most common single value.

On marketing data, the mode is almost always **zero**—which is itself the primary business finding!

:::
::::

. . .

**Decision Rule**: If you will multiply the summary by $n$ to forecast revenue or budget, you need the **mean**. For understanding user behavior on skewed data, start with the **median**.

## Spread & Percentiles: The Marketer's Habit {.smaller}

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

- **Standard deviation** assumes a symmetric bell curve and is dragged by outliers.
- On right-skewed marketing data, $\text{Mean} - 2\text{SD}$ routinely predicts negative values (e.g., $-15\text{s}$ duration or negative reach!).
- **Interquartile range (IQR)** ($Q3 - Q1$, or p25 to p75) is robust: it describes the middle 50% of your data.

. . .

**Build the p50 / p90 habit**:

> *"Average duration was 2m14s"* vs *"Half of visits ended in 20s; 1 in 10 lasted >4 minutes."*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/external/sd_bell_curve.png){fig-align="center" style="max-height:280px;"}

:::
::::

## The Bounce Problem & Five Honest Rules {.smaller}

Bounces are logged as 0 seconds duration and often constitute 50%–70% of website traffic. Mean duration is mostly a disguised bounce rate!

- **All Sessions** ($n = 500$, 320 bounces): Mean duration = **41s**
- **Engaged Sessions Only** ($n = 180$, bounces filtered): Mean duration = **114s**

. . .

**Five Rules of Honest Summary**:

1. **Plot the distribution before you summarise it.**
2. **Report a count ($n$) alongside every average and rate.**
3. **On skewed data, lead with the median and quote percentiles (p50 / p90 / IQR).**
4. **State explicitly which cohort or filter the summary covers.**
5. **If a summary changes a commercial decision, show the underlying distribution.**

# 2. The Four Families of Figures

## A Chart for Every Question {.smaller}

![](./figures/dd/viz_key_figures_1.jpeg){fig-align="center" height="340px"}

. . .

The variable types you have dictate the chart family:

- **1 Categorical** $\rightarrow$ **Composition** (*What is it made of?*)
- **1 Continuous** $\rightarrow$ **Distribution** (*What do the values look like?*)
- **Categorical + Continuous** $\rightarrow$ **Comparison** (*Does this group differ from that?*)
- **2 Continuous** $\rightarrow$ **Relationship** (*Does one move with the other?*)

## What a Figure Throws Away (Aggregation Zoo) {.smaller}

Every figure is an **aggregation** that chooses what summary to show and what to discard.

:::: {layout="[1,1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/viz_med_quartiles_1.png){height="170px"}

**Median & Quartiles**

Middle value + Q1/Q3 cutoffs. Interquartile range (IQR) forms the box.

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/viz_med_quartiles_2.png){height="170px"}

**Box Plot Anatomy**

Whiskers reach $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. Data points beyond are flagged as outliers.

:::

::: {#third-column}

![](./figures/dd/viz_correlation_1.png){height="170px"}

**Correlation & Regression**

Best fit line $Y = b_0 + b_1 X + e$. Pearson $r \in [-1, +1]$ measures linear strength.

:::
::::

# 3. The Four Families in Action & Tableau

## Family 1: Composition (Bar vs. Pie) {.smaller}

*What is this made of?* Counts or proportions across categories.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/loomrow/viz_pie_vs_bar.png){style="max-height:210px;"}

- **Pie charts**: Only acceptable for **two categories**, flat, directly labelled.
- Past 2 slices, human eyes cannot accurately judge angles. Bar charts communicate in one glance what pies conceal.

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_simple_bar.gif){style="max-height:210px;"}

- **Tableau Recipe**: Drag Dimension to Rows/Columns, Measure (or `CNT`) to the other shelf.
- **Rule**: Always sort bars descending by value!

:::
::::

## Family 2: Distribution (Histograms & Box Plots) {.smaller}

*What do the values look like?* Uncovering skewness, zero spikes, and spread.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_histogram.gif){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Histogram in Tableau**:

- Right-click Measure $\rightarrow$ **Create Bins...**
- Drag Bins to Columns, `CNT` to Rows.
- Reveals where the mass sits and where zero spikes occur.

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_box_plot.gif){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Box Plot in Tableau**:

- Drag Measure to Rows, disaggregate marks.
- Open **Analytics** tab $\rightarrow$ drag **Box Plot** to view.
- Avoid single "Average Bar" charts that hide the spread!

:::
::::

## Family 3: Comparison (Segmented Views) {.smaller}

*Does this group differ from that one?* Comparing performance across formats, channels, or campaigns.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_multiple_bar.gif){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Multiple Bars**:

- Add a second Dimension to **Color** for stacked bars, or Columns for grouped bars.
- Use percent of total when group sizes differ.

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_comparison_3.png){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Segmented Box Plots**:

- Place continuous metric on Rows, category on Columns.
- Instantly compares medians, spreads, and outliers across segments.

:::
::::

## Family 4: Relationship (Scatterplots & Trendlines) {.smaller}

*Does one move with the other?* Evaluating correlations and regressions between two continuous metrics.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_scatterplot.gif){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Scatterplot in Tableau**:

- Measure 1 on Columns ($X$), Measure 2 on Rows ($Y$).
- **Crucial**: Uncheck **Analysis $\rightarrow$ Aggregate Measures** (or add `post_id` to Detail) so Tableau doesn't sum to 1 dot!

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_relationship_2.png){style="max-height:210px;"}

**Trend Lines & Customization**:

- From **Analytics** tab, drag **Trend Line** into view. Hover to see $R^2$ and $p$-value.
- Use Marks card to encode third dimensions (Color, Size).

:::
::::

# 4. Visual Integrity: Principles & How Charts Lie

## Principle 1: Do Not Cheat With Axes {.smaller}

**Rule**: Include zero when zero is meaningful (bars, counts, rates). Truncating exaggerates trivial changes.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_2.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_3.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

*Wilke: Bar charts encode value by length/area. Truncating the axis magnifies differences dishonestly.*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_exercise_12.jpg){style="max-height:280px;"}

*KCRA News: A 5-cent gas price rise ($4.17 to $4.22) depicted as a 400% surge!*

:::
::::

## Principle 1 (cont.): Line Charts & Dual Axes {.smaller}

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_4.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_5.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

*Truncated baseline is legitimate for line charts of subtle variations (stock indices, temperature). Always disclose it!*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_6.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_7.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

***Never use two y-axes!** The scaling between them is arbitrary and invites false correlations. Two measures $\rightarrow$ two charts.*

:::
::::

## Principle 2: Make It Easy to Read {.smaller}

**Rule**: Sort bars by value, not alphabetically. Use horizontal bars for long labels.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_8.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_9.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

*Wilke: Horizontal bars prevent painful neck-straining rotated text. Sort bars by magnitude.*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_exercise_6.jpeg){style="max-height:280px;"}

*Georgia Dept of Health: Dates ordered **Apr 28, Apr 27, Apr 29, May 1** to manufacture an artificial downward decline!*

:::
::::

## Principle 3: Be Fancy Only When It Helps {.smaller}

**Rule**: Use transparency (alpha) for overplotting, jitter for discrete points. Avoid 3D effects and chartjunk!

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_10.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_11.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

*Wilke: Alpha transparency reveals density when points pile up.*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_exercise_3.jpeg){style="max-height:280px;"}

*Fox News: 3D pie chart slices that sum to 193%! (70% + 60% + 63%).*

:::
::::

## Principle 4: Colour Carries Meaning {.smaller}

**Rule**: Use a restrained palette. Color only what matters. Keep colors consistent across all dashboard sheets.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_16.png){style="max-height:150px;"}
![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_17.png){style="max-height:150px;"}

*Wilke: If "Reels" is blue on sheet 1, it must be blue across the entire dashboard.*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_exercise_1.png){style="max-height:280px;"}

*White House tweet: Highlighting one bar white and calling pandemic rebound "growth since 1984" (starting at 2001!).*

:::
::::

## Principle 5: The Details Are the Work {.smaller}

**Rule**: Direct labels beat remote legends. Title states takeaway. Geographic area $\ne$ human beings.

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_principle_20.png){style="max-height:280px;"}

*Wilke: Professional anatomy — informative title stating takeaway, units on axes, sample size ($n$), and data source.*

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/dataviz_exercise_11.gif){style="max-height:280px;"}

***Land does not vote; people do.** Animated cartogram scales counties by population rather than empty acreage.*

:::
::::

. . .

**The 4 Assignment Assessment Criteria (25% each)**:
- **Creativity (25%)**: Intuitive controls, dynamic filters, interactive actions
- **Analytical Depth (25%)**: Meaningful figure families, appropriate aggregations
- **Beauty & Design (25%)**: Clean layouts, intentional whitespace, harmonious palette
- **Overall Story (25%)**: Clear narrative guiding stakeholders to data-driven action

## Assembling the Dashboard in Tableau {.smaller}

Combine worksheets into an interactive command center:

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_dashboard.png){style="max-height:280px;"}

- Use **Horizontal** and **Vertical** layout containers to create a clean, responsive grid.
- Keep standard sizes (Fixed or Automatic).

:::

::: {#second-column}

![](./figures/dd/tableau_dashboard.gif){style="max-height:280px;"}

- Drag sheets into containers.
- Connect filters to multiple worksheets.
- Remove redundant legends to free up whitespace.

:::
::::

## Hands-On Exercise: The Honest Marketing Dashboard {background="#43464B" .smaller}

Using `insta-data.csv` in Tableau Public:

1. **Composition**: Build a bar chart of `theme` or `product_line` (counts and % of total).
2. **Distribution**: Build a histogram of `reach` (notice the severe right-skew!).
3. **Comparison**: Build side-by-side box plots comparing `reach` across `format` (reel, carousel, post).
4. **Relationship**: Build a scatterplot of `likes` vs `impressions` with a linear trend line.
5. **Assemble**: Combine the four sheets into a polished Dashboard with a clear title and business takeaway.

::: {#timer3_1 .timer seconds="1200" starton="interaction"}
:::

# 6. AI as a Statistical Critic

## Prompting the Statistical Critique {.smaller}

Assistants excel at *critiquing* statistical decisions when provided with distribution context:

> *"I reported mean session duration as 2m14s to the marketing director. Using the attached distribution (where 60% of sessions are 0s), write a rigorous critique explaining why this mean is misleading. Then list three clarifying business questions you would need answered before recommending an alternative summary metric."*

. . .

**Where AI Will Mislead You**:

- **Assumes Normality**: Defaults to t-tests and means without verifying distribution shape.
- **Blind to Domain Context**: Does not know 0s represent bounces unless explicitly told.
- **Silent on Sample Size**: Confidently interprets noise from tiny samples ($n = 12$).
- **Supplying business context is the analyst's un-delegatable job.**

## Exercise: The AI Statistical Audit {background="#43464B" .smaller}

1. Export summary statistics for `insta-data.csv` `reach`.
2. Ask AI: *"Critique reporting the mean reach of 9,788 vs the median of 5,184."*
3. Ask it what business risks arise if the ad budget is allocated based on the mean.
4. Evaluate its response: Which valid points did it raise? Where did it miss digital marketing nuances?

::: {#timer3_2 .timer seconds="600" starton="interaction"}
:::

## Going Further

- **Anscombe (1973)**, *Graphs in Statistical Analysis* — The foundational paper on why graphics are essential.
- **Matejka & Fitzmaurice (2017)**, *Same Stats, Different Graphs* — The Datasaurus Dozen.
- **Claus O. Wilke**, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* — Free online at [clauswilke.com/dataviz](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/)
- **Edward Tufte**, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* — "Above all else show the data."
